raw_response:
# C28 — catalogue-based candidate answer

I found four useful candidates. These are mechanisms to adapt, not claims that any candidate already implements the requested Swift feature. Discovery used opened awesome lists; verification used the selected projects or an original implementation article. The decision cutoff is 2016-01-26.

1. **libextobjc — EXTSelectorChecking**  
   Source: https://github.com/jspahrsummers/libextobjc  
   Catalogue: https://github.com/joeljfischer/awesome-apple  
   **Use:** Its receiver-aware compile-time selector check could inform a Swift expression that rejects a method identifier when the intended object does not declare that method.  
   **Caveat:** This is an Objective-C facility; adapting it to Swift would still require resolving the Swift-facing declaration to the Objective-C runtime name. The README establishes the check, but the source-directory open failed.  
   **Date:** Unknown. I did not establish a pre-cutoff version of this feature.

2. **Qt 5 — typed signal/slot references and generated metadata mapping**  
   Source: https://woboq.com/blog/how-qt-signals-slots-work-part2-qt5.html  
   Catalogue: https://github.com/JesseTG/awesome-qt  
   **Use:** Qt's checked member references and generated mapping to runtime signal indices provide a precedent for validating a class-qualified source declaration before producing an external runtime identifier.  
   **Caveat:** C++ member pointers and Qt's metadata machinery are not Objective-C selectors; Swift would need its own declaration-to-selector mapping.  
   **Date:** Pre-decision. The original implementation article is dated 2012-12-17.

3. **Djinni — generated cross-language interfaces**  
   Source: https://github.com/dropbox/djinni  
   Catalogue: https://github.com/fffaraz/awesome-cpp/blob/master/README.md  
   **Use:** Its shared interface descriptions and generated language-specific identifiers suggest keeping method identity and naming conversions in generated metadata instead of asking developers to reconstruct foreign spellings.  
   **Caveat:** Djinni targets C++ with Java or Objective-C and requires an interface description; applying the idea to arbitrary imported Objective-C methods would require importer integration or a new generator.  
   **Date:** Unknown for the verified implementation. The README mentions a 2014 introduction, but the linked slides failed and the video page exposed no transcript or publication date.

4. **R.swift — generated typed identifiers for string-addressed resources**  
   Source: https://github.com/mac-cain13/R.swift  
   Catalogue: https://github.com/uhub/awesome-swift  
   **Use:** Its generated, compiler-checked resource accessors suggest generating class-scoped Swift constants for imported method identifiers so misspellings become missing-symbol errors.  
   **Caveat:** R.swift generates resource accessors, not method selectors; this transfer would need method metadata, name-collision handling, and regeneration when imported APIs change.  
   **Date:** Later evidence. The opened README describes a September 2016 presentation and R.swift 7; I did not verify a pre-cutoff version.

The closest direct mechanism is libextobjc's receiver check; Qt supplies a dated example of combining source-level checking with runtime metadata. Djinni and R.swift offer generation-based alternatives. No candidate was tested, integrated, or shown useful in the target system.
